mcqs.question: What's the actual test for whether a component is worth building in-house, according to the answer skeleton?
options: Whether the team already has spare engineering capacity this quarter
Whether customers would choose this product over a competitor because of how well this specific thing is done
Whether the component is used constantly across the whole product
Whether a managed alternative exists on the market at all
mcqs.explanation: The skeleton's test for "core" is differentiation, not frequency of use or available spare capacity — a message queue is used constantly but rarely differentiates, while a niche ranking algorithm used in one feature can be the entire reason customers pick the product.

mcqs.question: A search-relevance company builds its own ranking system instead of using a managed search product. Why is this the right call despite the general bias toward buying commodity infrastructure?
options: Managed search products are always technically inferior to in-house systems
Building is always cheaper once a company reaches a certain size
The ranking logic is the company's actual differentiation, not commodity infrastructure around it
Regulatory requirements typically forbid using third-party search services
mcqs.explanation: The build-vs-buy call hinges on whether the component is core to differentiation, not on a blanket claim about technical quality, company size, or regulation — here the ranking logic literally is the product, which is exactly the case the general "buy commodity infrastructure" advice doesn't apply to.

mcqs.question: A managed service bought two years ago is now the company's biggest infra cost line. Was buying it originally the wrong call?
options: Yes, since hindsight shows it became too expensive, the original decision must have been flawed
No, since managed services should never be migrated away from once adopted
It depends only on whether a cheaper competitor product existed at the time
Not necessarily — it may have been correct for that stage, and a deliberate migration now is the correct next call, evaluated against today's constraints
mcqs.explanation: Two separate questions get conflated by hindsight: whether the original call was right given the constraints and needs at the time, and whether it's still right now. Both can have different, individually correct answers — the escalating cost line argues for a deliberate migration today, not that the original buy decision was a mistake.

mcqs.question: A team defaults to building every infrastructure component in-house because "we might need custom behavior someday." What's the actual cost of this stance?
options: An ongoing operational tax — patching, scaling, on-call — paid continuously for flexibility that's usually never used
None, since building in-house is always strictly better for engineering morale
It only affects hiring, since more engineers are needed to build everything
It's a one-time cost paid during the initial build and nothing further
mcqs.explanation: The cost isn't a one-time build expense or purely a morale/hiring question — it's the continuous operational burden of owning something long-term, paid every day, in exchange for a speculative flexibility benefit that in most cases never actually gets exercised.
